summary: For the privileged-admin wedge I can fund this from the PAW/second-laptop hardware line with a hard-dollar CFO case. Beyond that it is a nice-to-have competing with VDI and lockdown. A kernel-level hypervisor from an unproven startup on every bank endpoint needs compatibility, performance, independent security assurance and vendor-viability proof first; the 500-seat minimum misfits the wedge.

objections.objection: Outside privileged users there is no must-have driver. Locked-down endpoints are an accepted cost; 'employee frustration' does not win budget against audit findings. The fleet-wide case (open_questions) is unproven, so spend is capped at the small privileged population.

The 500-endpoint minimum ($100k/yr) can exceed the number of privileged admins in many target firms, so the wedge buyer is asked to pay for seats they cannot deploy, or to commit before a pilot proves the product.

Approval risk: a bare-metal hypervisor under the corporate OS touches every endpoint agent, the patch cycle and the help desk. If it breaks laptops, I own that outage. Bank vendor-risk management will require third-party pen tests, source escrow and financial-viability evidence that a 20-person startup lacks at first.

No buyer-side evidence in the input. There are no interviews, budget data or quantified dual-laptop costs, and the problem evidence is encyclopedia pages, so the ROI claim 'cheaper than a second laptop or VDI' is asserted rather than shown.

Microsoft's own PAW guidance can be implemented with tools I already license (Windows security features, Intune, Defender), so the CFO will ask why we can't do a dedicated device or native hardening instead of adding a new vendor.

strongest_point: There is a hard-dollar, CFO-friendly case for admins carrying two laptops: $200/year replaces roughly $1,000+ in hardware plus support. That spend can come from an existing PAW budget.
what_would_change_my_mind: At least 4 of 10 bank/tech CISOs commit to paid 50-seat pilots with named budget (the concept's own test).
A TCO model from real dual-device fleet costs at 3 customers shows more than 40% savings.
Pilots show compatibility with incumbent EDR/management agents and no measurable help-desk ticket increase.
An independent security assessment passes a bank vendor-risk review.
The minimum is lowered to fit privileged-user counts.
